text.tspan: Everyday English - C1 - 2026/03/20 - Essay - 01
A calendar gives plans a place in time.
Pexels · 20657557
Looking back and looking ahead
The decision to make a realistic plan may appear ordinary, yet it exposes a recurring tension between arrangements that make life manageable and
experiences that resist being prescribed. A defensible approach combines proportionate preparation with a willingness to reconsider whose interests a
plan serves.
Preparation has value because reviewing a specific experience teaches more than a vague judgement. In the present case, we describe one habit that
helped us instead of calling the whole year good or bad. Such an intervention is modest, but that modesty is its strength: it removes a foreseeable obstacle
without claiming to determine the entire experience. Structure is useful to the extent that it releases attention rather than consuming it.
That argument requires a qualification, however: a small next step is easier to act on than a broad promise. For instance, we choose a ten-minute practice
session and put it on the calendar. An arrangement that appears efficient from one standpoint may impose costs elsewhere. Listening to those affected is
therefore not an optional gesture of goodwill; it supplies information without which the plan cannot be adequately evaluated.
The resulting principle is one of proportion. Preparation deserves support when it clarifies responsibilities and protects time, while responsiveness
prevents it from hardening into an end in itself. To judge the experience well is to examine both what the arrangement enables and what it may
inadvertently exclude.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the conclusion. Each body paragraph
needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Write about an attempt to make a realistic plan that did not go as planned. Explain two lessons, each supported by a specific incident. Use four short
paragraphs: introduction, two developed points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: introduce the situation; discuss reviewing a specific
experience teaches more than a vague judgement with an example; discuss a small next step is easier to act on than a broad promise with a different
example; conclude by connecting the two points.)
